question: What is another common medical name for psychomotor epilepsy?
explanation: Psychomotor epilepsy starts mainly in the temporal lobe, so doctors and nurses commonly call it temporal lobe epilepsy. You've got this! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h1)

question: What does 'mesial temporal sclerosis' mean in temporal lobe epilepsy?

options.A: Scarring and neuron loss in the hippocampus
options.B: A sudden blockage of the carotid artery
options.C: Bleeding into the ventricles of the brain
options.D: Inflammation of the outer brain lining

explanation: Think of mesial temporal sclerosis as scarring deep inside the temporal area (the hippocampus). This damage makes it easier for abnormal electrical storms to start. Keep pushing forward! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h1)

question: Which of these is a very common cause of epilepsy in tropical regions like Nigeria?
explanation: Severe infections like cerebral malaria can harm brain tissue. The resulting scars can later spark seizures. Excellent clinical knowledge to carry into your wards! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h2)

question: A patient with psychomotor seizures has a history of a severe car accident two years ago. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Head injuries can disrupt brain pathways and leave scar tissue behind, which acts like a tiny spark plug for seizures later on. You are learning fast! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h2)

question: What is an 'aura' when someone has a focal seizure?

options.A: A sudden spike in body temperature
options.B: A complete loss of all skeletal muscle tone
options.C: A total paralysis of one side of the body
options.D: A subjective warning sign experienced before awareness is impaired

explanation: An aura is actually a mild seizure on its own that serves as a warning bell before the main seizure takes over the patient's full awareness. Well done! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h3)

question: Which behavior is a classic example of an automatism during a psychomotor seizure?

options.A: Sudden falling backward with stiffened limbs
options.B: Repetitive lip-smacking and fumbling with buttons
options.C: Sustained rhythmic shaking of both lower limbs

explanation: Automatisms are automatic, repetitive actions like smacking the lips, swallowing, or picking at clothes while the patient's mind is cloudy. Spotting these makes you a sharp nurse! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h3)

question: Which imaging scan is best for spotting hippocampal scarring in psychomotor epilepsy?
explanation: An MRI gives a clear, high-resolution picture of soft brain tissues, making it the top choice for finding tiny scars or shrinking in the hippocampus. Great job! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h4)

question: Why is information from family members so important when diagnosing seizures?

options.A: Relatives can perform bedside electroencephalogram tests at home
options.B: Family members are legally required to sign consent for medication trials
options.C: Patients often have amnesia for the events and cannot describe the seizure themselves
options.D: Patients exaggerate their symptoms when alone

explanation: Because patients usually don't remember what happened during or right after the seizure, family members or witnesses are vital for filling in the story. You're mastering patient assessment! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h4)

question: What is the main goal of taking anti-seizure medications?

options.A: Eliminating the need for any future medical follow-ups
options.B: Curing the underlying genetic mutation permanently
options.C: Inducing deep sedation to prevent all physical activity
options.D: Achieving complete seizure control with minimal side effects

explanation: Anti-seizure drugs aim to stop abnormal brain waves so the patient can live a normal, seizure-free life without feeling heavily drugged. Keep up the brilliant study habit! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h5)

question: What dangerous emergency can happen if a patient abruptly stops taking their anti-seizure medication?
explanation: Stopping anti-seizure drugs suddenly can trigger a dangerous loop of continuous seizures called status epilepticus. Patient education on compliance is a major nursing duty! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h5)

question: When is a patient usually considered for epilepsy surgery?

options.A: Only when the patient refuses to take any pills at all
options.B: Immediately upon receiving the first diagnosis of a seizure
options.C: When seizures persist despite trying multiple appropriate medications
options.D: When the electroencephalogram shows a normal brain pattern

explanation: Surgery is saved for drug-resistant cases where standard medications have been tried properly but still haven't stopped the seizures. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of a vagus nerve stimulation device in epilepsy care?

options.A: To permanently cure the structural brain scar
options.B: To completely stop all electrical activity in the brain
options.C: To replace the function of damaged temporal lobe tissue
options.D: To reduce how often and how severe seizures occur

explanation: Think of a vagus nerve stimulator as a gentle pacemaker for the brain that helps dial down the frequency and intensity of seizures when drugs aren't enough. Brilliant! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h6)

question: A patient starts having a psychomotor seizure while sitting on a chair in the ward. What should you do immediately?

options.A: Force a padded tongue depressor firmly between the teeth
options.B: Restrain the arms tightly to stop the automatic movements
options.C: Ease the patient to the floor and clear nearby hazardous objects
options.D: Leave the room immediately to call the attending physician

explanation: Patient safety is job number one! Guiding them gently to the floor prevents nasty falls and bumps against furniture. You're going to be an amazing ward nurse! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h7)

question: Why is it dangerous to put objects into the mouth of a seizing patient?

options.A: It increases the electrical voltage inside the brain
options.B: It triggers immediate cardiac arrest in all patients
options.C: It can damage teeth, cause oral trauma, or obstruct the airway
options.D: It permanently stops the postictal confusion phase

explanation: Trying to force items into a seizing patient's mouth often breaks teeth, hurts their gums, or blocks their breathing tube. Never put anything in their mouth! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h7)

question: What does the medical acronym SUDEP stand for in epilepsy?

options.B: Severe unprovoked disorder of electrical pathways

explanation: SUDEP refers to the rare and tragic sudden death of a person with epilepsy where no other clear cause can be found. Keep up your steady study routine! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h8)

question: Which nursing action helps most with the social and emotional challenges of chronic epilepsy?

options.A: Focusing solely on medication dosages and ignoring emotional health
options.B: Isolating the patient from family to reduce external stress
options.C: Encouraging the patient to hide their diagnosis from employers
options.D: Providing counseling resources and addressing social stigma

explanation: Epilepsy carries a lot of societal stigma in many communities. Offering support, education, and counseling helps patients build confidence and live full lives. You've got this! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h8)
